content: Baycol (cerivastatin) was withdrawn from the market due to reports of potentially fatal rhabdomyolysis, a severe adverse reaction involving muscle damage associated with this cholesterol-lowering medication. The FDA has endorsed and supported this decision. Patients currently taking Baycol are advised to consult their healthcare providers to discuss alternative treatment options. Cerivastatin is a medication that reduces blood cholesterol levels by inhibiting the enzyme in the liver responsible for cholesterol production. It effectively lowers total cholesterol and the LDL (bad) cholesterol fraction, which is a major contributor to the development of coronary artery disease. Reducing LDL cholesterol levels can slow or even reverse the progression of coronary artery disease. Cerivastatin belongs to the same drug class as atorvastatin (Lipitor), simvastatin (Zocor), pravastatin (Pravachol), lovastatin (Mevacor), and fluvastatin (Lescol). It was approved by the FDA in 1997. Cerivastatin tablets should be stored at room temperature, between 15°C and 30°C (59°F to 86°F). Cerivastatin is prescribed for the treatment of high blood cholesterol. Initial management of elevated cholesterol typically involves lifestyle modifications such as exercise, weight loss, and a diet low in cholesterol and saturated fats. If these measures fail to adequately reduce cholesterol levels, medications like cerivastatin may be introduced. The National Cholesterol Education Program (NCEP) has established treatment guidelines for the use of such drugs, which recommend therapy based on LDL cholesterol levels and the presence of other risk factors, including diabetes, hypertension, smoking, low HDL (good) cholesterol, and a family history of early coronary heart disease. The cholesterol-lowering efficacy of cerivastatin is dose-dependent, meaning higher doses result in greater reductions in cholesterol levels. Blood cholesterol levels are monitored regularly during treatment to allow for dose adjustments. Cerivastatin is typically taken once daily at bedtime and can be administered with or without food. The risk of muscle damage, including rhabdomyolysis, is increased when cerivastatin or other drugs in its class are used concurrently with certain medications, such as cyclosporine, gemfibrozil, erythromycin, itraconazole, and nicotinic acid. It is presumed that cerivastatin interacts similarly with these drugs. The safety of cerivastatin during pregnancy is not well established. It may be used during pregnancy if the prescribing physician determines that the potential benefits outweigh the risks. Similarly, it is unknown whether cerivastatin is excreted in breast milk. Physicians and patients must carefully weigh the benefits and risks of using cerivastatin in nursing mothers. Cerivastatin is generally well-tolerated, with side effects being rare. Minor side effects may include constipation, diarrhea, fatigue, gas, heartburn, nasal congestion, and headache. Caution is advised when using cerivastatin in patients with liver diseases, including those related to alcohol use. Persistent abnormalities in liver function tests during treatment are uncommon but may necessitate discontinuation of the medication. Rare cases of muscle damage due to inflammation (myositis) have been reported with other drugs in the same class and are presumed to occur with cerivastatin as well. Muscle inflammation can lead to the release of myoglobin, a muscle protein, into the bloodstream, which may result in kidney failure.
